notes: \cpara{Defines the error: expecting a process whose causal structure differs from a human brain's to do what your own brain predicts.}

\cpara{Recalls the example from ``The Tragedy of Group Selectionism'' (November 2007), which ``The Hidden Complexity of Wishes'' also used: biologists before 1966 who believed predators would restrain their breeding to spare their prey.}
\cpara{Explains the theory: groups that restrained their breeding would survive and send out colonists, so restraint would spread.}

\cpara{Summarizes, without repeating, the case against the theory made in the earlier post: no evidence, predator populations that crash, and mathematics that makes the required conditions nearly impossible.}
\cpara{Asks whether the theory's originators were doing something wrong.}
\cpara{Voices the objection that they could not have known before the experiment.}
\cpara{Introduces Wade's laboratory test of group selection.}

\cfact{Wynne-Edwards's own summary of his theory is less peaceful. ``Individuals are made to compete for the right to feed''; those who fail ``emigrate, or get killed by predators, disease, or starvation,'' and ``surplus adults are inhibited from breeding'' (his commentary on the 1962 book in ``This Week's Citation Classic,'' 1980). ``Quiet peace with enough food for all'' is not how he described it.}

\cpara{The result, in the words of the earlier post. As noted on ``The Hidden Complexity of Wishes,'' Wade's abstract lists cannibalism as one of four changes, and I could not find the source of ``especially female larvae.''}
\cpara{Says that in hindsight the result is obvious: selection for small groups favors eating other individuals' children.}
\cpara{Asks why the group selectionists did not think of it. The question assumes they did not; on the evidence about Allee's school, see the note on ``The Hidden Complexity of Wishes.''}
\cpara{Answers with a human case: a tribe facing scarcity would propose one child per couple, and would not even think of cannibalizing each other's daughters.}
\cpara{Describes the brain as a search process that produces solutions ranking high in your own preferences.}
\cpara{Adds that because the space of solutions is large, an efficient brain does not even formulate most low-ranking ones.}
\cpara{Illustrates: you do not consider hopping on one leg; your search goes straight to agreements about family size.}
\cpara{Concludes that cannibalism would not be generated by a human search.}
\cpara{The key step: ``low'' and ``high'' belong to the process doing the preferring, and different processes search in different orders.}
\cpara{Applies it to evolution, for which cannibalism is favored and restraint is not. The remark on search order is hedged (``seem around equally simple'').}
\cpara{Imagines the error made openly: ``I would do it this way,'' so evolution will.}
\cpara{Turns to the author's own field, AI, and says what people do not reply when told an AI will not necessarily work as they do. The claim rests on the author's experience; no reply is quoted.}
\cpara{Says what they reply instead: a reason why any AI, or natural selection, must do what occurs to a human as a good idea.}
\cpara{Presents group selection theory as a reply of that kind.}
\cpara{The central claim about the biologists: they kept the conclusion of the open error and replaced the reasoning above it with rationalizations.}

\clogic{This describes how particular scientists reached their theory, and the post gives no record of it. No work by Wynne-Edwards, Allee or Brereton is quoted; the process is inferred from the conclusion. The one first-hand account I found, Wynne-Edwards's commentary of 1980, says the idea came while he was reviewing David Lack's book on the natural regulation of animal numbers. That does not settle the question either way, and the post cites nothing.}
\cpara{Asks why a scientist would do this, since the data came out against them.}

\cpara{Answers with an evolutionary story from ``Fake Optimization Criteria'' (November 2007): people descended from those who argued best that the tribe's interest required their rival's death. Here it is hedged (``seem to have evolved'').}

\cpara{Adds that we evolved to believe these arguments sincerely, because sincere arguers persuade better. The hedge of the previous paragraph is gone, and no evidence has been added. The idea is a hypothesis; von Hippel and Trivers argued a version of it at length in 2011, three years after the post.}
\cpara{Applies the story to the group selectionists, in a mocking voice. It rests on the account of their reasoning questioned above.}
\cpara{Says why the arguments failed: evolution has nothing that could be moved by an argument.}
\cpara{Closes the example: reality came out differently.}
\cpara{Names the post's real subject in one sentence. The step from evolution to AI is left to the reader.}

\cpara{Generalizes: optimism is ranking outcomes by your preferences and taking the top one as a prediction, while the process being predicted does not use your ranking. The warning is sound in the post's own ``not necessarily'' form.}
